abstract: We examine optimal non-cooperative monetary policy in a two-country New Keynesian setting with complete financial markets and pricing to market for goods.In contrast to the case in which the law of one price holds for goods, currency misalignments are an important consideration even for selforiented policymakers.Financial markets are critical in the analysis.Under "full" commitment, the optimal policy considers the effects on asset values and hence wealth distribution across countries.Optimal policy under full commitment differs from the "partial" commitment case in which the policy commitment is not made until after asset markets clear.Surprisingly, the optimal targeting rule under strategic policy with full commitment is the same as under cooperative policy.In this setting, changes in state-contingent claim prices offset the wealth a self-oriented policymaker might seek through terms-of-trade manipulation, and we show that there are no gains from cooperation.Although a policy chosen under partial commitment may be desirable from a country's perspective, the resulting Nash equilibrium yields lower welfare.
focus_rationale: A theoretical two-country New Keynesian model with complete financial markets and pricing to market; it is not tied to any particular economies.

title: HouseholdBench: Evaluating Large Language Models as Predictors of Household Economic Behavior
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to meet a key goal in economics: a quantitative model of household decision making, across a variety of settings.Yet existing evaluations cover few surveys and outcomes, and do not study how households adjust to changing economic conditions.We introduce a new evaluation, HouseholdBench, which unites 6 U.S. household surveys and 32 prediction tasks spanning numeric, categorical and probabilistic outcomes, related to consumption, income, labor, expectations, and housing.Using past behavior, demographics and macroeconomic conditions, the tasks test whether LLMs predict behavior, including how households adjust to changes in various policies.We evaluate 13 proprietary and open-weight LLMs against a no-change baseline and a gradient boosted tree model.Most LLMs outperform the no-change baseline, including for policy response tasks-with the best model lowering error for numeric outcomes by 12.2%.Across most tasks, gradient-boosted trees rank first; leading proprietary LLMs approach their performance, but open-weight models lag.LLMs exhibit systematic over-and underprediction across different tasks.We identify methods that enable a 4 billion parameter open-weight model to match proprietary models' performance: fine-tuning and aggregating 16 predictions per observation.Improvements generalize to policy-response tasks, which are excluded from fine-tuning.We release our datasets, code, and leaderboard on our website.
focus_rationale: The paper evaluates LLM predictions of household behavior using US household surveys and US macroeconomic conditions, so it is mainly about the United States.

title: A Bayesian analysis of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model
abstract: The Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model (CIR) is a diffusion process with widespread applications in economics, finance and population biology. In this paper we first obtain a full Gibbs Sampler for the exact CIR process observed at equidistant times. We do not require the imposition of the Feller condition. We show how to carry out smoothing and handling of missing data. Additionally, the introduction of a tailored single Metropolis-Hastings step allows us to handle irregular and random time intervals. Secondly, we obtain several asymptotic properties which include Local Asymptotic Normality, consistency and asymptotic normality of conditional maximum likelihood estimation and a Bernstein-von Mises theorem. Lastly, we provide an empirical illustration using U.S. Treasury yields under a variety of priors and a comparison with other models such as the Vasicek and the 3/2 models.
focus_rationale: The empirical illustration uses U.S. Treasury yields, so the paper is mainly about an advanced economy, with the methods applying to interest-rate dynamics generally.

title: New England’s Rural Economy: An Overview
abstract: In New England, as in most of the country, rural communities account for a sizable majority of the land but a relatively small portion of the population and employment. Nevertheless, rural communities make important contributions to the region’s economy, particularly in the agricultural sector. This brief provides a high-level overview of rural New England, comparing it with the region’s urban counties and with the country’s rural counties.
focus_rationale: The paper studies rural and urban counties in New England, a region of the United States, so it is advanced-economy focused.

title: Inflation Expectations in the Context of Climate Change and the Green Transition
abstract: This paper studies how views on climate change shape household inflation expectations. Us-ing a new representative survey of Dutch households, we elicit perceptions of climate change, the green transition and climate policies, and their expected effects on long-run inflation. House-holds expect climate change, the green transition and three types of climate policies – carbon pricing, support for the green transition and support for green innovation – to raise inflation and inflation volatility over the next ten years. Climate change is expected to have the largest effect, while support policies are expected to have the smallest. These results suggest that climate-related beliefs are linked to the anchoring of inflation expectations and that support policies for the green transition and green innovation may facilitate the net-zero transition while keeping in-flation expectations relatively well anchored. We also document significant heterogeneity across households. Expected inflationary effects of climate change are larger among respondents who anticipate more severe global warming and extreme weather. Climate-related inflation concerns are widespread across demographic groups.
focus_rationale: The paper uses a representative survey of Dutch households, so it studies the Netherlands, an advanced euro area economy.

title: Chokepoints in global supply chains: lessons from rare earths and hard disk drives
abstract: Concentration and limited substitutability can turn the efficiency gains from global supply chains into vulnerabilities. However, the consequences of chokepoints depend on their underlying nature.
focus_rationale: The paper examines supply chain chokepoints using rare earths and hard disk drives as cases, without a specific country focus. It is a cross-sector, global topic.

title: Macroeconomic Effects of Forced Displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of forced displacement on host economies in SubSaharan Africa, drawing on cross-country panel data and country case studies of Burkina Faso, South Sudan, and Uganda to provide granular evidence on the consequences of spatial concentrations of forcibly displaced persons within countries. Estimates from a difference-in-differences local projections (LP-DiD) framework do not suggest that large refugee inflows significantly affect host-country GDP, inflation, or the current account balance over a five-year horizon. The effects on the primary fiscal balance also appear to be muted, yet this masks offsetting fiscal dynamics: government expenditures rise and fiscal revenues increase (mainly through taxes). These results are robust to restricting the control group to Sub-Saharan African economies. Under a broader treatment definition that captures the total displaced population (refugees and internally displaced persons), the GDP response turns significantly negative and intensifies with displacement severity, though this estimate is best interpreted as an upper bound because it cannot be fully separated from the effects of conflict itself that generates displacement. The cross-country findings are consistent with the case studies, which indicate generally muted effects on aggregate food inflation and wages. Beneath this muted aggregate response, however, a consistent pattern emerges across cases: prices of imported and processed staples rise, while those of locally produced cereals stay flat or fall. The case studies also yield mixed evidence regarding the impacts of displacement inflows on consumption and labor force participation, with such inflows reducing host employment in Burkina Faso but raising it in Uganda.
focus_rationale: The paper studies host economies in Sub-Saharan Africa (Burkina Faso, South Sudan, Uganda) plus a cross-country SSA panel, so it is clearly emerging/developing-market focused. Its macro outcomes (GDP, inflation, current account, fiscal balance) give an indirect market link.

title: Global Spillovers from U.S. Bond Supply Shocks
abstract: I study spillovers from U.S. bond supply shocks, identified from yield moves around U.S. Treasury auction announcements. Using the shocks as instruments in daily and monthly local projections for AEs and EMs, I find substantial pass-through to global long-term rates. A debt expansion shock that raises the U.S. 10-year yield by 10 bps lifts foreign 10-year yields by roughly 7 bps within a few business days. Monthly aggregation shows contractionary real effects: U.S. industrial production falls up to 0.4 percent after eight months and foreign industrial production by a comparable amount, around 0.4 percent, with a more persistent profile. The foreign contraction reflects financial tightening, exchange-rate depreciation, and weaker U.S. demand. Spillovers are heterogeneous: moving from the 25th to 75th percentile of foreign investor participation deepens the IP decline by 0.5 pp. Results are robust to a demand-side shock and consistent with the relevant benchmarks, highlighting U.S. bond supply as a key driver of global financial conditions and real activity, amplified by foreign investor participation and weak domestic fundamentals.
focus_rationale: The paper studies spillovers from U.S. Treasury bond supply to both advanced and emerging economies' long-term rates, FX and real activity, so it covers AEs and EMs together.

title: The EU’s Energy Transition and Fuel Price Shocks
abstract: This paper analyzes how achieving Europe’s medium-term greenhouse gas mitigation targets enhances energy security, defined as the cushioning of the adverse macroeconomic impact of oil and gas price shocks. It uses the IMF’s Global Macroeconomic Model of the Energy Transition, which combines a rich set of New-Keynesian features with a detailed representation of fossil fuel use, including granular modelling of the transport and heating sectors. Future oil and gas price shocks are simulated in a scenario where Europe’s mitigation policy agenda has been fully implemented (and mitigation targets are met), and in a hypothetical scenario where mitigation policy has remained constant at the current level of ambition. A comparison shows that the policy agenda substantially dampens future shock transmission. The inflationary impact of both shocks is close to 40 percent larger under constant policies than under the mitigation agenda, and for oil shocks, the output decline is about twice as large. These energy security co-benefits materialize gradually as the economy adjusts to the mitigation agenda, and are shown to depend on ETS2, the new emissions trading system covering transportation and buildings. An additional exercise proxies for merit-order electricity pricing. In these simulations, the mitigation agenda further reduces pass-through from gas price shocks to electricity prices, thereby enhancing the macroeconomic stabilizing effects.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the euro area and Europe's energy transition, with oil and gas price shock transmission to inflation and output in Europe.

title: Information Networks and Inflation Expectations
abstract: How are inflation expectations affected by foreign supply shocks? We show that, beyond bilateral exposure, a second network matters: the one linking forecasters to the countries they cover. Using forecasterlevel expectations around conflict episodes—precisely dated supply shocks that raise inflation through trade and energy linkages—we find that expectations are revised upward gradually in the days following a conflict. Within the same country and day, forecasters who cover the conflict country revise by 0.2 to 0.3 percentage points less than those who do not, and the differential roughly triples where bilateral exposure is highest. We rationalize this in a model where a public narrative overstates spillovers in proportion to bilateral exposure, and only forecasters covering the conflict country can discount it. The consensus therefore inherits a bias largest where exposure is high and coverage thin, and a central bank reading it at face value tightens more than fundamentals warrant.
focus_rationale: The paper uses forecaster-level expectations across many countries around global conflict-driven supply shocks, so it covers multiple economies rather than a single advanced or emerging group.

title: Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance: Bridging Policy, Research and Practice
abstract: The challenges that climate change poses to the financial system require bringing together the knowledge and experience of central banks, policymakers, academics and experts. In this context, on 25 March 2026, the Banco de España organised the conference “Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance: Bridging Policy, Research and Practice”, together with the Network for Greening the Financial System, the Centre for Economic Transition Expertise and the Transition Pathway Initiative Centre at the London School of Economics. The main contributions are presented in this joint publication by the Banco de España and the journal Papeles de Energía published by Funcas.
focus_rationale: This is a conference compilation on climate risk and sustainable finance with no specific economy singled out in the abstract, so it covers the topic across countries and institutions.

title: Global-to-UK SVAR
abstract: This paper investigates how global shocks transmit to the UK economy. We build a Global-to-UK Bayesian structural vector autoregression model that identifies five global shocks using sign, ranking, and bound restrictions. We find that these shocks account for around half of the variation in UK GDP and CPI over the first year. World energy and world financial shocks are the main global drivers of UK inflation and economic activity overall, while world financial shocks explain most of the variation in fluctuations in Bank Rate. Building on the identified global shocks, we extend the analysis and investigate their transmission across a panel of advanced and emerging economies. Focusing on a common global financial shock, we find that responses are larger in more financially open economies, particularly for exchange rates and equity prices.
focus_rationale: The paper's core is how global shocks transmit to the UK economy, with the UK as the main focus, though it extends to a panel of advanced and emerging economies.

title: Lighting the shadows: central bank policy transmission through banks and non-banks
abstract: Non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) account for an increasingly large share of credit provision and play a central role in quantitative easing (QE). We develop a DSGE model with banks, NBFIs and a central bank interacting through wholesale deposits, bonds and reserve markets to study how monetary transmission changes as the size of NBFIs expands. We estimate the model on UK data to evaluate key parameters in the financial sector. We find that the transmission of conventional interest rate policy to output and inflation is essentially unaffected by the size of the NBFI sector. Conversely, the transmission of QE is strongly altered by the size of the NBFI sector and the source of its expansion. When the NBFI sector expands due to firm funding preferences, this amplifies QE. When it expands due to an increased cost of obtaining bank finance, transmission is largely unchanged. The results underscore that monetary policymakers retain rate control regardless of financial structure, but that the effectiveness of balance sheet policies depends on the composition and behaviour of the non-bank sector.
focus_rationale: The paper estimates a DSGE model on UK data, studying monetary transmission and QE through banks and non-bank financial institutions in the UK.

title: News shocks and inflation: theory and evidence from large oil discoveries
abstract: We study hownews shocks affect inflation in open economies, using large oil and gas discoveries with realized production lags of at least five years as observable news about future output. Panel local projections show that discoveries raise core consumer prices over the subsequent decade, with about half the increase occurring prior to extraction.
focus_rationale: The paper uses a cross-country panel of large oil and gas discoveries across open economies, so it covers multiple countries without a specific focus on advanced or emerging markets.

title: Understanding Over-Optimism in Tax Revenue-to-GDP Forecasts under IMF-supported Programs
abstract: Revenue mobilization is a key objective in many IMF-supported programs, yet tax revenue-to-GDP forecasts often fall short of outcomes. This paper analyzes the underlying drivers of these forecast misses by leveraging two novel global datasets on tax policy yields and tax administration capacity. It finds that tax revenue-to-GDP forecast errors are primarily driven by over-optimism in forecasted yields of tax policy measures and tax buoyancy assumptions, as well as macroeconomic forecast errors, particularly for growth and trade openness. Stronger tax administration capacity and well-implemented and high-quality revenue related structural reforms are associated with lower forecast errors. Additional empirical analysis shows that over-optimism in forecasted tax policy yields declines significantly when revenue measures are well-designed, part of large-measure revenue packages, and accompanied by high-quality revenue-related structural reforms. Improving forecast realism requires better-grounded yield estimations and tax buoyancy assumptions, explicit consideration of implementation capacity, and a focus on well-designed revenue-related structural reforms.
focus_rationale: The paper uses global cross-country datasets on IMF-supported programs without restricting itself to one group of economies, so it is Transversal.

title: Recurring Natural Disasters and Macroeconomic Scarring
abstract: Recurring climate-related natural disasters pose significant macroeconomic and fiscal risks for highly exposed countries. We extend the Debt, Investment, Growth, and Natural Disasters (DIGNAD) model to incorporate Annual Average Loss (AAL) metrics, capturing the cumulative macro-fiscal effects of repeated natural disaster shocks. The augmented DIGNAD framework introduces recurring annual capital losses and negative productivity shocks, yielding more realistic growth and public debt trajectories under persistent disaster risk. We quantify the GDP losses from recurrent natural disasters and examine the trade-offs between higher adaptation investment (leading to higher recovered growth) and public debt accumulation. Using cross-country simulations for 33 disaster-prone economies and case studies (the Philippines, Mauritania, and Barbados), we find substantial heterogeneity in disaster impacts and adaptation effectiveness. Comparing risk-adjusted baseline projections with scenarios of scaled-up resilient vs. standard infrastructure investment, we find that investing in resilient public capital can significantly mitigate output losses in the long-term, albeit at the cost of higher public debt.
focus_rationale: The paper simulates 33 disaster-prone economies, with case studies on the Philippines, Mauritania and Barbados, which are mainly emerging or developing economies. It focuses on macro-fiscal scarring and public debt rather than market pricing.

title: The Global Fiscal Actions (GFA) Dataset
abstract: We introduce the Global Fiscal Actions (GFA) Dataset, the first quarterly global narrative database of discretionary fiscal policy actions, covering 142 countries since 1990. GFA combines Economist Intelligence Unit country reports with large language models to systematically identify and classify tax and spending measures, together with their motivations, timing, implementation status, and supporting evidence. We validate the dataset against economists' assessments, existing narrative datasets, fiscal aggregates, and repeated AI extractions, demonstrating high accuracy and reproducibility. We illustrate its value through applications to fiscal cyclicality and country-specific fiscal multipliers, providing new evidence on the conduct and effectiveness of fiscal policy worldwide.
focus_rationale: The dataset covers 142 countries worldwide, spanning both advanced and emerging economies, so it has no single market focus.

title: Effectiveness of Monetary Policy Transmission in Morocco amid Reforms to the Monetary Policy Framework
abstract: This paper assesses the effectiveness of Morocco’s monetary policy transmission since 2018 in light of reforms aimed at modernizing the policy framework. Over the past decade, Morocco has introduced greater exchange rate flexibility, strengthened the legal and operational focus on price stability, and enhanced central bank communication—measures intended to anchor inflation expectations and improve transmission. Drawing on several years of post-reform data, we use a two-step empirical strategy: (i) identifying exogenous monetary policy shocks through a Taylor-rule-based approach leveraging Bank Al-Maghrib’s forecasts, and (ii) estimating their dynamic effects via local projections, a flexible approach well suited to settings with structural change and limited data. Our findings indicate that transmission to output and inflation has strengthened post-reform: a 1 percentage point policy rate hike reduces output by about 0.3 percent and inflation by 0.1 percent, compared to 0.1 and 0.05 percent pre-reform, respectively. However, responses remain delayed and muted relative to benchmark estimates for other emerging markets. Analysis of transmission channels shows the interest rate channel is most active, the credit channel is partially effective, and the exchange rate channel is stronger post-reform, while the asset price and expectations channels remain weak. These findings provide important insights for Morocco’s ongoing transition to an inflation targeting regime.
focus_rationale: The paper studies monetary policy transmission to output and inflation in Morocco, an emerging market, including the interest rate, credit and exchange rate channels.

title: Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option
abstract: We investigate a dynamic oligopoly model with two phases: a normal phase where an essential input is available, and a disruption phase where firms must rely on inventories. Disruptions create an overcutting pricing incentive arising from the option to forgo sales and monopolize the market once rivals stock out. This monopoly option causes the price to jump to a supracompetitive level at the advent of the disruption and to remain above the competitive price path throughout. Price caps raise welfare, but reduce inventory investment. Government reserves reduce prices and raise buffer stocks, as do reserve mandates when financially feasible.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical dynamic oligopoly model of supply disruptions and pricing with no specific economy studied, so it is Transversal.

title: Perspectives on Iberian Economic Integration
abstract: María Alejandra Amado Garfias, João Amador, Sónia Félix, Joana M. Garcia, Vanda Geraldes da Cunha, Corinna Ghirelli, Ángel Luis Gómez Jiménez, Eduardo Gutiérrez Chacón, Cristina Manteu, Luis Molina Sánchez, Enrique Moral-Benito, Sergio Puente Díaz, Javier Quintana González, Martín Saldías, Sharmin Sazedj, Sofia Terlica and Jacopo Timini
focus_rationale: The paper concerns economic integration between Spain and Portugal, both euro area advanced economies. The abstract lists only authors, so the specific economic channels studied cannot be confirmed.

title: The Energy Assistance Landscape: Programs to Reduce Utility Cost Pressures
abstract: A survey of federal and local programs looks at help available to low-income Eighth District households for paying utility bills, weatherizing homes and improving energy security.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
focus_rationale: The paper surveys US federal and local energy assistance programs for low-income households in the Eighth District, a US Federal Reserve region.

title: WP - 2026-10-23 - Severin Joho and Enzo Rossi: The evolution of frequency, language complexity and policy narrative: benchmarking Python-based NLP and ChatGPT on a century of SNB rhetoric
abstract: We compiled and processed a novel, comprehensive dataset of 1,063 speeches delivered by high-ranking Swiss National Bank officials between 1928 and 2024. Beyond tracking their quantitative evolution, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the length, readability and thematic content. To ensure robust results, we benchmarked traditional Python-based NLP text mining against generative artificial intelligence using ChatGPT. Our findings highlight four primary policy insights. First, the frequency of annual speeches has followed an upward trajectory since the mid-1950s, accelerating notably after the transition to flexible exchange rates. Second, a clear shift toward brevity is evident. Third, the language has become increasingly accessible since the 1960s. Fourth, inflation has moved to the forefront of the thematic discourse in the era of flexible exchange rates, while cyclical economic development and unemployment have received less emphasis. Finally, we outline key methodological lessons for deploying LLMs to analyze central bank communication, emphasizing the complementary relationship between probabilistic language models and deterministic Python frameworks, while addressing inherent algorithmic pitfalls and identifying critical open questions for future research.
focus_rationale: The paper studies a century of speeches by Swiss National Bank officials, so it is about Switzerland, an advanced economy.

title: How Closely Do Public and Private Labor Market Data Align for New England Compared with the Nation?
abstract: The use of private labor market data for research and policy work at the Federal Reserve and elsewhere has prompted discussion about how they align with public data at the national level. However, there has been less assessment of such alignment at the regional level, where patterns may differ given distinct sample sizes, market features, and other factors. This brief’s analysis indicates that private labor market data for New England or the New England states are generally less aligned with corresponding public data compared with the alignment of private and public data for the United States as a whole.
focus_rationale: The paper studies New England states and the United States as a whole, both advanced-economy labour markets, comparing private and public labour market data.

title: Short-time work, its replacement rate and labour mobility
abstract: Short-time work schemes, such as Italy's Cassa Integrazione Guadagni (CIG), support workers' earnings and help firms preserve jobs during downturns, but they may also reduce mobility towards more productive and financially stronger firms. This paper assesses how the CIG replacement rate (the ratio of the benefit to the employee's wage) affects job-to-job mobility, using administrative data on workers and firms in Italy for 2008-19. A 10-percentage-point increase in the replacement rate raises the probability that a worker remains with the same employer by about 3 per cent. The effect is stronger for workers with lower individual productivity. The additional fiscal cost associated with the resulting reduction in moves towards better-performing firms is relatively small.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Italy's Cassa Integrazione Guadagni short-time work scheme and worker mobility using Italian administrative data, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: Superbonus and work injuries in the construction sector in Italy
abstract: The Superbonus led to a rapid and substantial increase in economic activity in Italy's construction sector. Periods of expansion of this kind typically entail an increase in workplace injury rates. This paper examines whether the rise in construction employment induced by the Superbonus was accompanied by a change in the construction injury rate. Between 2021 and 2023, the Superbonus led to an increase in construction employment and, contrary to expectations, a decline in the rate of severe workplace injuries. The effect was stronger in the regions where the incentive was used more extensively. It is plausible that firms strengthened preventive measures, since violations of workplace safety regulations could have resulted in the loss of this substantial incentive.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Italy's construction sector and the Superbonus fiscal incentive, so it is an advanced-economy study.

title: Beyond the surface: investor base, risk-taking and fragility in open-end funds
abstract: This paper examines how an investment fund's investor base can affect its ability to cope with a sudden increase in redemptions. To this end, it exploits as a natural experiment the sharp decline in Italian government bond prices in 2018, which prompted Italian insurance companies to redeem shares in bond funds in order to mitigate the impact of the decline on their solvency ratios. As a result, these funds experienced liquidity pressures that were unrelated to their own performance. Our analysis shows that funds with a predominantly long-term investor base were able to offset redemptions by Italian insurance companies by attracting new inflows, without changing the risk profile of their portfolios. By contrast, funds held mainly by short-term investors did not fully offset the redemptions and increased the riskiness of their assets, likely in an attempt to attract more performance-sensitive investors.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Italian bond funds and Italian insurance companies during the 2018 sell-off in Italian government bonds, so it is about a euro area member economy.

title: The concentration channel of the minimum wage
abstract: This paper analyses the potential effects of introducing a minimum wage in the Italian economy through a general equilibrium model in which firms hold both monopsony power in the labour market, due to job search frictions, and monopoly power in the product market, owing to imperfect substitutability between goods. Introducing a minimum wage would reduce the number of small, less productive firms while increasing the market share of larger ones. This would be accompanied by growth in average labour productivity and wages, alongside a modest rise in unemployment. The reallocation of market shares towards larger firms would raise average profit margins (a concentration channel). For very high minimum wage values, this would compress both the labour share of GDP and the expansionary effects of the minimum wage.
focus_rationale: The paper models the Italian economy specifically, so it is DM. It studies the effects of a minimum wage on firm concentration, productivity, unemployment and profit margins.

title: Capital quality and regional disparities: evidence from commercial vehicle transactions
abstract: The study analyses territorial differences in the quality of motor vehicles owned by Italian companies, using a database of commercial and industrial vehicle transactions between 2015 and 2024. The quality of these vehicles is measured on the basis of age and environmental efficiency. Firms in the South and Islands purchase older and less environmentally efficient vehicles on average and keep them in service for longer than firms in the North. The characteristics of firms and vehicles account for about one third of the territorial differences in the quality of these goods. The gap is also due to the pronounced territorial segmentation of the second-hand market, which limits the flow of newer vehicles from the North to the South.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Italian firms and the commercial vehicle market across Italy's North and South, an advanced euro area economy.

title: Beyond firm size: network position and shock transmission in firm-to-firm production networks across five economies
abstract: This paper compares supplier networks in Italy, Belgium, Estonia, Hungary and Portugal using harmonized data on transactions between firms. It examines the distribution of buyer-supplier relationships, firms' positions in the production chain, and how these networks shape the transmission of shocks, especially monetary policy shocks. The analysis shows that trade between firms is concentrated in a small number of buyer-supplier relationships. It also finds that supplier networks are substantially less interconnected than sectoral input-output tables suggest. Firms' positions in the production chain help explain how shocks are transmitted: simulations for Italy and Belgium indicate that upstream firms contribute more to changes in final product prices following monetary tightening.
focus_rationale: The paper studies firm-to-firm supplier networks in five economies: Italy, Belgium, Portugal and Estonia (euro area) and Hungary (non-euro CEE). The mix of advanced and emerging-type economies makes it Transversal.

title: The Welfare Impacts of Urban Renewal and Forced Relocation: Evidence from Chicago’s HOPE VI Demolitions
abstract: This paper studies one of the largest spatial redevelopment efforts in the United States: HOPE VI public housing demolitions. Focusing on Chicago, we estimate a neighborhood choice model combining administrative records tracking displaced public-housing residents with Census Bureau data capturing citywide sorting and prices. Demolitions generate large welfare losses driven by displacement costs, partially offset by housing vouchers. Demolitions also raise housing prices and reshape neighborhood composition, with gains concentrated among higher-income homeowners. Counterfactuals show that more generous vouchers and counseling programs mitigate but do not eliminate displaced residents’ losses, while expanded redevelopment yields larger citywide gains through general-equilibrium effects.
focus_rationale: The paper studies public housing demolitions and neighborhood sorting in Chicago, a US city, so it is clearly advanced-economy focused.

title: Stress testing European banks’ transition risk and lending behavior
abstract: As the financial sector grapples with climate-related risks, central banks and regulators are increasingly using climate stress tests ( CSTs ) to assess banks’ resilience and encourage climate-sensitive lending practices. This study investigates whether the European Central Bank’s ( ECB ) 2021–22 CST influenced how euro area banks price loans based on borrowers’ carbon intensity. The findings reveal that while the CST did not uniformly alter loan pricing, it triggered significant portfolio reallocation and differential pricing strategies, shedding light on how supervisory tools can shape the financial sector’s role in the low-carbon transition. How do climate stress tests influence banks’ lending behavior? Introduction Banks are pivotal in financing the transition to a low-carbon economy, but they also face significant risks from climate change. These include transition risks, which arise from policy changes and shifts in market preferences, and physical risks, stemming from climate-related disasters. To address these challenges, the ECB conducted its first EU - wide CST in 2021–22, aiming to assess banks’ preparedness for climate risks and encourage better integration of these risks into their governance and lending practices. This paper examines whether the CST influenced banks’ loan pricing and credit allocation, particularly with respect to borrowers’ greenhouse gas ( GHG ) emissions intensity. Methodology The authors use granular loan-level data from the Eurosystem’s AnaCredit database, which provides detailed information on bank loans to non-financial corporations. Borrower-level GHG intensity is estimated using sectoral emissions data and firm turnover, allowing the study to capture transition risk exposure across a broad range of firms, including small and medium-sized enterprises. The analysis employs a difference-in-differences (DiD) framework, comparing changes in the sensitivity of loan spreads to borrower carbon intensity for banks subject to the CST (treated banks) versus those not subject to it (control banks). The study also decomposes the observed effects into intensive (within-relationship repricing) and extensive (portfolio reallocation and entry/exit) margins. Theoretical Framework The paper builds on a theoretical model in which a CST acts as an information-revelation shock, shedding light on transition risks and increasing supervisory scrutiny. This shock alters banks’ perceived risk distribution, influencing their lending decisions. The model predicts that CSTs can steepen, flatten, or leave unchanged the relationship between loan spreads and borrower carbon intensity, depending on how banks adjust their pricing and portfolio composition in response to the new information. Key Findings Aggregate Effect on Loan Pricing : On average, the CST did not significantly change the sensitivity of loan spreads to borrower carbon intensity. The post- CST shift in the spread–intensity slope was small and statistically indistinguishable from zero. Portfolio Reallocation : Treated banks reallocated credit away from more carbon-intensive incumbent borrowers, reducing their share of new lending to these firms. This reallocation was particularly pronounced among the most carbon-intensive borrowers. Entry/Exit Pricing : Treated banks charged higher spreads to new borrowers with higher carbon intensity compared to incumbents, about 10 bps more for one SD increase in carbon-intensity. This is evidence of more stringent pricing of transition risks on the extensive margin. Intensive Margin : Within existing bank–borrower relationships, there was little evidence of systematic repricing based on carbon intensity. This suggests that the CST ’s impact operated primarily through portfolio composition rather than within-relationship adjustments. No significant Heterogeneity in Treatment Intensity : Among significant institutions ( SIs ), banks that participated in the more demanding bottom-up module of the CST did not exhibit stronger changes in carbon-sensitive pricing compared to those that only participated in lighter modules. This suggests that the main behavioral adjustments stemmed from CST participation itself, rather than the depth of the exercise. Asymmetric and Nonlinear Effects : Treated banks responded more strongly to decreases in borrower carbon intensity than to increases, and the CST ’s impact was more pronounced for borrowers in the upper tail of the emissions distribution. Conclusion The ECB ’s CST influenced banks’ lending behavior primarily through portfolio reallocation and differential pricing of new relationships, rather than through uniform changes in loan pricing. Treated banks reduced their exposure to carbon-intensive borrowers and applied more stringent pricing to new high-intensity relationships, signaling a shift toward climate-sensitive credit allocation. However, the CST ’s impact on within-relationship repricing was limited, highlighting the importance of relationship dynamics and informational frictions in shaping banks’ responses to climate risks. From a policy perspective, these findings suggest that CSTs can serve as effective tools for encouraging banks to integrate climate risks into their lending decisions, even in the absence of direct capital requirements. By revealing transition risks and increasing supervisory scrutiny, CSTs can drive portfolio adjustments that align with broader climate goals. Future research could explore the real-economy implications of these adjustments, such as their impact on firm-level emissions and investment, as well as the interaction between CSTs and other climate policies. De Bandt, O., D. Nefzi, J.-G. Werner (2026), Stress testing European banks’ transition risk and lending behavior, Bundesbank Discussion Paper, No 33/2026.
focus_rationale: The paper studies euro area banks and their loan pricing to non-financial corporations using AnaCredit data, which makes it a DM paper.

title: Bank liquidity regulation and the growth of private credit
abstract: We study the role of bank liquidity regulation in the growth of private credit. Following the introduction of the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), private credit increases significantly more in U.S. counties with a larger footprint of banks subject to the LCR or of LCR banks with greater initial liquidity shortfalls.
focus_rationale: The paper studies U.S. counties and U.S. banks subject to the liquidity coverage ratio, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
abstract: Foreign aid has become a melting pot of motivations and policies, where differently-motivated actors often converge on recommended policies while the similarly-motivated diverge.Breaking down the "why" and the "how" can illuminate real tensions and reveal false ones.The "why" asks which problems to tackle and who benefits: the recipient, the donor through economic, political, or soft-power returns, or everyone through global public goods.The "how" asks which strategy most cost-effectively addresses a chosen problem.Evidence is central to the "how": use it where it exists, produce it where it does not.In particular, approaches which improve state capacity to use and generate evidence can satisfy multiple objectives: strengthen recipient countries, benefit donors, and provide a global public good of knowledge.Ultimately, the "how" is not a linear process, but rather an iterative one of learning, adopting, adapting, repeating, and then sharing so others can learn as well.
focus_rationale: The paper is a conceptual framework on foreign aid motivations and strategies across donors and recipients, with no particular economy or country group as its focus.

title: Correcting for Heterogeneity in the Use of Subjective Scales
abstract: Analyses of survey data may be confounded if people use response scales differently.We formalize and generalize the theory behind using "calibration questions," such as vignettes, to correct for scale-use heterogeneity.Finding, in our (N 10,000) and existing data, that the mapping between respondents' scales is approximately linear, we develop a simple estimator for scale-use-corrected regressions.We validate it using subjective-scale ratings of height and weight and illustrate it with life satisfaction regressions, where correction leaves the main qualitative findings intact but can substantially change coefficient ratios, for example tripling the estimated cost of unemployment relative to income.
focus_rationale: The paper is a methodological contribution on survey response-scale heterogeneity, validated with height and weight ratings and illustrated with life satisfaction regressions, without a particular economy as its focus.

title: Too Little too Late? Nationwide Carbon Trading in China
abstract: China launched a nationwide, rate-based carbon market in 2021.Covering the world's top CO2 emitter, compliance depends on the intensity of carbon emissions rather than an absolute cap.We draw on the theoretical literature of rate-based systems to provide the first empirical evidence on an early adopter.Using plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning methods, we find that high-efficiency power plants increased electricity generation and CO2 emissions by approximately 5% relative to low-efficiency plants.Because its carbon market regulates nearly all coal plants in China, we focus on the differential responses by plant efficiency, finding no evidence of a differential reduction in emission intensity (though these estimates are imprecise).Relative to coal plants in Indonesia and the Philippines, which had no carbon market, China's high-efficiency plants also increased emissions, while the estimate for its low-efficiency plants is small and insignificant.This pattern of responses suggests that emissions increases of highefficiency plants exceeded substitution away from low-efficiency plants.Underscoring the production stimulus to more efficient Chinese plants, air quality worsened downwind of highefficiency plants relative to low-efficiency plants, compromising air quality in relatively clean areas of China.If China's goal is to reduce its carbon emissions, then benchmarks will need to be tightened within the existing system or an alternative system that does not simultaneously incentivize electricity production will need to be adopted.
focus_rationale: The paper studies China's nationwide rate-based carbon market and its effect on coal power plants, with comparison to Indonesia and the Philippines. Its link to markets is indirect, via energy, emissions policy and the carbon market's design.

title: Will Medical Care Strangle or Save the Federal Budget?
abstract: Forecasts of the federal budget depend greatly on trends in medical spending.Since 1970, medical spending has nearly tripled as a share of gross domestic product (GDP).However, spending growth has barely exceeded GDP growth since 2010.This difference in growth rates makes forecasting spending difficult.I present scenarios for future spending derived from considering the sources of spending increase, ranging from rapid increases in new, expensive treatments to a reduction in spending due to cost-reducing technology.Even modest increases in spending relative to GDP are likely to overwhelm the federal government's ability to pay for medical care using current tax instruments.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US federal budget and medical spending as a share of GDP, a fiscal sustainability question for an advanced economy.

title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers' skills.We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training.The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development.We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions.We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs.This in turn makes general skill firm-specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.
focus_rationale: The abstract describes firm-level training data and a theoretical knowledge hierarchy model with no specific economy named, so it is cross-country or theoretical in focus.

title: Venture Capital and Customer Capital
abstract: Venture capital specializes in the financing of customer capital intensive firms-firms with higher sales and marketing expense to revenue ratios, a higher wage bill for sales and marketing employees, and a higher tendency to apply for trademarks-and they do so more than other financial intermediaries.Venture capitalists target high customer capital industries with low knowledge capital but avoid high knowledge capital industries that lack customer capital.Firms tilt investment toward customer capital leading up to the initial venture capital investment, after which their scale accelerates rapidly.Venture capitalists focus on financing customer capital because such investments require tolerance for substantial risks of failure in pursuit of extreme upside potential, as characterized by power law returns.This return profile fits customer capital investments more closely than investments in knowledge capital.Venture capitalists that sprinkle small investments across a large number of firms, colloquially referred to as the "spray and pray" strategy, target customer capital industries for investment, whereas venture capitalists that commit larger amounts to a small number of firms target knowledge capital industries.The venture capital focus on customer capital reflects a shift away from its traditional focus on knowledge capital intensive firms over the past 30 years.
focus_rationale: The abstract describes US venture capital and firm-level data on customer capital, which points to a US-centred study of advanced-economy firms rather than a cross-country or emerging-market sample.

title: Firms' Investment and the Real Transmission of the Global Financial Cycle
abstract: We study how global financial conditions transmit to firms' investment.We document that increases in risk premia are followed by large investment contractions, particularly among firms with higher default risk.We develop a quantitative heterogeneous-firm open-economy model where firms finance investment with defaultable debt priced by risk-averse global investors.We identify a strong risk channel linking changes in the global price of risk to financing costs through firms' quantity of risk-the sensitivity of debt repayment to global shocks.This introduces a risk dimension to stabilization policy: smoothing cash flows reduces firms' quantity of risk and dampens international financial transmission.
focus_rationale: The abstract describes a cross-country open-economy model and global financial conditions transmitted to firms, without a specific emerging or advanced economy focus in the summary. It is global in scope.

title: The Effects of a Shorter Workweek on Employment, Output, and Productivity
abstract: Do shorter workweeks generate work-sharing and productivity gains, as intended by policymakers?We study France's pay-preserving reduction in the workweek from 39 to 35 hours, bundled with employer payroll tax cuts.We first exploit the staggered implementation by firm size to identify the impact of the reform package.We then use differential exposure to the hours cut and tax cut to separate their effects.We combine matched employer-employee, balance-sheet, and survey data to study worker, firm, and local labor market effects.The reform package left employment unchanged.This zero masks large offsetting effects: absent the tax cuts, the shorter workweek would have reduced employment by 3.8%.The effects are skill-biased, raising employment among managers and professionals while reducing it among other employees.Finally, shorter hours raised total factor productivity by 2%, limiting the output decline to 1% despite a 6% fall in total hours.Surveys point to work intensification and organizational changes as potential drivers of productivity gains.
focus_rationale: The paper studies France's 2000s-era workweek reduction and payroll tax cuts, an advanced economy, with labour market, employment and productivity effects.

title: Transportation as a Barrier to Education Access: Evidence from Chicago Public Schools
abstract: School choice can weaken the link between residential neighborhood and educational opportunity only if students can reach the schools available to them.We study school choice in Chicago, where high schoolers can choose among schools throughout the city but generally rely on public transit, making the structure of the transit network a key determinant of opportunity.Using student-level rankings and public transit travel times, we document two systematic patterns: Black students are less likely to rank top-rated schools first and face longer public transit times to such schools.We estimate a discrete choice model to separate the value placed on schools from the costs of reaching them.We find that high schools vary substantially in how they are valued and that there is a high degree of agreement across racial groups in their relative ranking.However, transit times vary significantly across neighborhoods, generating racial differences in demand for top-rated schools.Counterfactually, giving Black students the travel times of white students increases demand for top-rated schools by 23 percentage points.Finally, we identify underserved neighborhoods where public transit access constrains demand and quantify how targeted bus service would increase demand for high-quality schools.Our counterfactuals quantify how transportation expands school access.
focus_rationale: The paper studies high school choice and transit access in Chicago, a US city, with no macro or financial angle.

title: The Impact of the Great Recession on Mortality: A Dynamic Factor Analysis
abstract: We use a dynamic factor time series model to estimate the national mortality impact of the Great Recession.In aggregate, the Great Recession reduced the average annual, age-adjusted mortality rate by about 2 percent, with effects persisting for at least a decade.In a calibrated model of the welfare effects of the estimated impacts of the Great Recession on consumption and mortality, we find that the welfare gain from the estimated mortality decline is quantitatively significant relative to the welfare loss from the estimated consumption decline.The estimated mortality decline is also quantitatively close to prior mortality estimates using cross-sectional variation in the severity of the Great Recession, implying limited general equilibrium effects of the Great Recession on mortality.More broadly, our findings suggest that prior evidence from local labor markets that recessions are good for health can be extrapolated to the likely mortality consequences of nationwide recessions.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the United States and the national mortality effects of the Great Recession, so it is advanced-economy focused.

title: Upgrading Financial Markets
abstract: Expanding access to financial services may not be enough to develop markets in low-income settings: providers also need to be held accountable to consumers.We test this in a field experiment across 195 rural Sierra Leonean communities, upgrading Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs) into mobile money and bank agents, cross-randomized with a monthly consumer feedback mechanism.Upgrading expands access, but feedback drives large operational improvements (+20.5 pp, 85%), particularly in privacy and consumer protection, raising usage and revenues.Upgraded VSLAs also show higher savings digitization and higher incomes, evidence that disciplining agent actions benefits not only consumers but also the principal that finances and stands behind its agent.Interpreted through a framework of delegated intermediation, we show accountability, not infrastructure alone, aligns provider incentives with consumer welfare and is central to designing scalable financial intermediaries.
focus_rationale: The paper is a field experiment in rural Sierra Leone, a low-income economy, studying mobile money and savings agents. It has little link to rates, FX or sovereign markets, though it touches on financial access and intermediation.

title: Green Subsidies with Demand Distortions
abstract: Credit constraints and other demand distortions are pervasive in lower-income contexts.A model of clean technology adoption shows that demand distortions can increase the welfare gains from green subsidies.This arises through two channels: shifting the marginal adopter toward higher private and social benefits, and increasing demand elasticity.We test this by cross-randomizing purchase price subsidies, usage subsidies, and access to an interest-free loan for a US$84 induction stove among 2,134 charcoal users in Kenya.Usage subsidies of 75% have a precise zero effect on adoption and usage.Purchase price subsidies, however, generate large welfare gains.Credit constraints raise the subsidy's efficacy by 35%-73%, up to US$10-US$12 in observable welfare gain per subsidy dollar.This demand distortion also lowers the subsidy cost of abatement by 41%, to US$12 per tCO 2 e.This operates through the two channels identified in the theory: credit constraints raise the marginal adopter's positive externality by 19% and fuel savings by 30%, and lower the subsidy cost per marginal adoption by 29%.In a counterfactual without demand distortions, the abatement cost rises to US$137 per tCO 2 e. Contexts with large demand distortions could offer many cost-effective opportunities for climate change mitigation financing.
focus_rationale: The paper is a field experiment with charcoal users in Kenya on clean cooking subsidies; it studies an emerging economy but has no direct market or macro focus.

title: The Robust Properties of Economies with Endogenous Production Networks
abstract: We characterize equilibria in a canonical class of economies with endogenous production networks, showing that log-prices equal a min-max over networks of a primitive affine function of logproductivities.This formula captures how resilience and fragility interact: the "min" reflects resilience from substituting suppliers, while the "max" reflects fragility from complementarityinduced rigidity.Applying these results, we generalize Hulten's theorem, finding that local Domar weights are generally insufficient to describe propagation of even small shocks.Moreover, we characterize how microeconomic volatility affects GDP, finding that smooth changes in Domar weights overstate its adverse effects by omitting option value from switching suppliers.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical characterization of general equilibrium economies with endogenous production networks, with no particular country focus.

title: The Impact of Social Insurance on Household Debt
abstract: This paper investigates how the expansion of social insurance affects households' accumulation of debt.Insurance can reduce reliance on debt by lessening the financial impact of adverse events such as illness and job loss.But it can also weaken the motive to self-insure through savings, and households' improved financial resilience can increase access to credit.Using data on 10 million people and a quasi-experimental research design, we estimate the causal effect of expanded insurance on household debt, exploiting ZIP-level heterogeneity in exposure to the staggered expansions of one of the largest US social insurance programs: Medicaid.We find that a 1 percentage point increase in a ZIP code's Medicaid-eligible population increases credit card borrowing by 0.38%.Decomposing this effect in a model of household borrowing, we show that increased credit supply in response to households' improved financial resilience drives the rise in borrowing and contributes 30% of the net welfare gains of expanding Medicaid.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US households and the effect of Medicaid expansion on credit card borrowing and household debt in the United States.

title: Pricing Power in the Mortgage Market: Evidence from GSE Fee Waivers
abstract: Market power may arise not only from firms, but also from individual salespeople who can exploit informational advantages over consumers.We explore this phenomenon in the mortgage market by examining a Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac fee waiver targeted at lower-income first-time homebuyers.We estimate that mortgage intermediaries capture over 60% of $1.5 billion in total fee waivers during 2023-2024, rather than fully passing these savings through to borrowers.Pass-through varies substantially across loan officers: those with a track record of originating expensive mortgages (independent of lender pricing) pass through less than 20% of the waiver.Our evidence suggests that loan officers retain incentives to steer borrowers into higher-rate mortgages, despite post-crisis regulations designed to limit such practices.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the US mortgage market and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac fee waivers, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: Home-Foreign Elasticity Functions and the Gains from Trade
abstract: Gains from trade are typically calculated using a constant trade elasticity estimated from substitution across foreign countries.For general homothetic preferences, we show how to calculate these gains from the initial domestic expenditure share and the home-foreign elasticity function along a price path to autarky.While this function generally depends on the specific price path, under weak separability it does not.We provide conditions for its nonparametric identification and estimate sector-level elasticity functions using tariff changes implied by trade agreements.Across WIOD and OECD ICIO data, estimated home-foreign elasticities generally rise with domestic expenditure shares.Using estimated elasticity functions in a multi-sector model with intermediate inputs, the median gain across the WIOD countries is 19.37 log points, compared with 24.43 when each country-sector elasticity is held fixed at its initial value.
focus_rationale: The paper develops a general theory of gains from trade and estimates sector-level elasticities across WIOD and OECD ICIO country data, covering many economies rather than one region.

title: Credit Markets with New Screening Technologies
abstract: We study equilibrium market structure in a model of credit-market competition with correlated or uncorrelated screening errors and endogenous screening technologies.A pool externality arises because rejected borrowers reapply elsewhere, so lenders' screening and pricing choices affect competitors' applicant pools.With independent errors, a single market segment emerges, with rates rising smoothly as lenders who choose better technologies lend to more adversely selected borrowers.With correlated screening errors, potentially stemming from similar AI systems and overlapping financial-sector data, ex-ante identical lenders instead specialize across qualitatively distinct segments, generating a hockey-stick interest-rate schedule: segments with uniform rates but heterogeneous borrower quality coexist with segments featuring uniform quality but dispersed rates, echoing traditional banking, fintech, and high-rate indiscriminate lending.We show how technological and regulatory changes affecting screening costs, including frontier AI innovation and various forms of open banking, unevenly affect financial access and can either benefit or harm financially excluded borrowers.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical model of credit-market competition with no specific economy studied, so it is Transversal.

title: Are We Consuming Too Much Groundwater?
abstract: We study the optimality of human groundwater extraction from many of the world's 3,400 aquifers, where institutional or market failures may produce non-optimal extraction decisions.We use remote sensing and economic data to estimate a dynamic model of water extraction for each aquifer, recover the discount factor that rationalizes observed groundwater extraction, and compare it against Ramsey and market benchmarks.Three-to four-fifths of aquifers are extracted more rapidly than is optimal, decreasing aquifer present value by several percent, and creating trillions of dollars in present value welfare losses.Policies that guarantee users constant water quantities indefinitely, through subsidies or prior appropriation, or policy rules that fully discount future extraction, generate larger welfare costs.A sustainable extraction path that maintains current fill forever generates meaningfully lower welfare than the optimal extraction path, because most aquifer stocks are already inefficiently low.
focus_rationale: The paper studies groundwater extraction across many of the world's aquifers worldwide, a global cross-country sample rather than a focus on either advanced or emerging economies.

title: From Politics to Process: Evidence from Progressive Era Naturalizations
abstract: States that delegate governance to local officials face a trade-off between the benefits of local knowledge and the costs of biased administrators.Can imposing federal standards discipline bias and improve uniformity?We study this question by examining the introduction of federal standards to apply for citizenship under the 1906 Naturalization Act.Using newly-digitized census records covering over five million immigrants and a 30-year period, we show that standardizing adjudication of citizenship applications resulted in rapid convergence of naturalization practices across cities.While naturalizations were around 30% higher in election years pre-reform, this electoral cycle disappeared after the introduction of federal standards.Exploiting the staggered adoption of municipal civil service reforms aimed at removing patronage during the Progressive Era, we find that the reduction in political cycles was strongest in unreformed cities.Finally, the contraction in election year naturalizations changed the composition of new citizens.Affected cohorts earned 7% more, were more likely to enter citizenship-restricted occupations, and gave children more Americanized names.Our results thus show that standardizing administrative procedures can discipline politically-biased policy implementation.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US city-level naturalization practices during the Progressive Era under the 1906 Naturalization Act, so it is about the United States.

title: A Model of U.S. Monetary Policy and the Global Financial Cycle
abstract: We propose a general equilibrium model in which U.S. monetary policy affects global risk premia by revaluing the wealth of currency-mismatched arbitrageurs.Assuming their portfolios are meanvariance efficient, arbitrageurs must be short the dollar.A U.S. tightening thus erodes arbitrageurs' net worth and raises the global price of risk.We discipline this mechanism to rationalize the effects of U.S. monetary policy on international asset prices, and we quantify the associated macroeconomic spillovers and role of policy responses abroad.In a potential future with higher dollar interest rates, arbitrageurs' dollar funding and U.S. monetary policy spillovers are dampened.
focus_rationale: The model is a general equilibrium framework about how U.S. monetary policy drives the global financial cycle through global risk premia and dollar funding of arbitrageurs, with no single economy as the focus. It is cross-country in scope and theoretical in method.

title: Modeling and Evaluating the Labor Market and Fiscal Effects of Immigration
abstract: Immigration affects natives through both labor markets and public budgets, yet these channels are usually studied separately.We combine them in a general-equilibrium model with search-andmatching frictions, skill-specific progressive labor taxes, capital taxation and public goods, calibrated to 17 OECD countries over 2015-2019.The welfare effect on natives of a onepercentage-point increase in immigrant inflows varies in sign and size across countries, hinging on immigrants' skill mix, immigrant-native wage gaps, resident unemployment, and tax progressivity.For inflows matching the skill composition of 2019-2024 arrivals, native welfare rises in 14 of 17 economies, and in most cases both skill groups gain, through different channels.Lower-skilled natives gain mainly from higher pre-tax earnings, driven by job creation and complementarity with skilled immigrants; higher-skilled natives gain mainly from lower labor-tax burdens.Evaluating immigration policy thus requires modeling labor-market and fiscal channels jointly: either channel alone gives an incomplete picture of who gains and why.
focus_rationale: The paper calibrates its general-equilibrium model to 17 OECD countries, which are mainly advanced economies, so it is DM. The abstract does not name individual countries.

title: Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
abstract: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed "genealogy" of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1887 and 2024.By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale inputoutput network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States.We report four main findings.First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 54% of U.S. technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologies rely on foreign inputs most heavily.Second, foreign ideas have large causal effects on U.S. innovation.Using the historical settlement of migrants as a source of exogenous variation in local ancestry, we show that U.S. counties more exposed to knowledge from a given foreign country absorb substantially more technologies from that country and, in turn, invent significantly more U.S. technologies building on them.Third, foreign ideas shape not only the level but also the direction of technical change: U.S. counties are far more likely to pioneer the specific technologies whose foreign inputs are already in their local idea stock, and the changing origins of foreign ideas accompany the shift of American innovation from its historical heartland toward the coasts.Fourth, these effects leave a lasting imprint on local labor markets: decades later, counties that absorbed more of an origin's ideas host more jobs working with those ideas, and even more work with the U.S. technologies descended from them.
focus_rationale: The paper studies how foreign technologies feed U.S. innovation and local U.S. labour markets, so its focus is the United States, an advanced economy.

title: The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act
abstract: This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion.Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies.Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025).This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act's wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature.We estimate that California's billionaires contribute $3.3-5.8 billion annually in state income taxes.The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion.Across 100,000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.
focus_rationale: The paper studies a California state wealth tax and billionaire migration within the United States, an advanced economy.

title: Export Controls and the Economics of National Security
abstract: Export controls restrict trade to limit adversaries' access to goods that contribute to military capability, but their effectiveness depends on how trade and production adjust across countries.We combine new data on U.S. export control classifications and licensing outcomes with a quantitative general equilibrium model featuring dual-use production, input-output linkages, and separate civilian and military final expenditure.We estimate large export and entry frictions from these controls.These effects are substantially smaller for U.S. exports to members of multilateral export control regimes (MECRs): the differential is equivalent to an export cost of 15 to 29 log points.Relative to a counterfactual without differential controls on adversaries, multilateral controls reduce their imports of controlled products far more than unilateral U.S. controls.Only 7% of the reduction in controlled exports under the multilateral regime is replaced by other countries, compared with 28% under unilateral U.S. policy.Multilateral controls reduce adversaries' real military expenditure by increasing their military price index.The security impact, measured as U.S. real military expenditure relative to adversaries, rises by about 1 log point under multilateral controls but only 0.14 log points under unilateral controls, with both imposing a similar civilian real cost.Even a U.S. embargo fails to reproduce the multilateral security outcome.
focus_rationale: The paper studies U.S. export controls and their effects on trade flows and military expenditure across U.S. exports, multilateral regime members and adversary countries, so it is cross-country rather than focused on one market group.

title: Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-led Interviews
abstract: The advent of large language models (LLMs) creates new opportunities to conduct qualitative interviews at scale, with thousands of respondents, thereby bridging qualitative and quantitative methods. We develop a simple, versatile approach for researchers to run AI-led qualitative interviews, including voice interviews. We assess its robustness by drawing comparisons to human experts and with several respondents-based quality metrics. The versatility of the approach is illustrated through four broad classes of applications: eliciting key factors in decision making, political views, subjective mental states, and mental models of the effects of public policies. High performance ratings are obtained in all of these domains. Our applications highlight the potential of AI-led interviews as a tool for measurement, hypothesis generation, and discovering mechanisms.
focus_rationale: The paper is a methodological contribution on AI-led qualitative interviews with applications to decision making, political views and policy mental models, with no specific economy studied.

title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information
abstract: Decisions are typically made by drawing on multiple sources of information, yet the correlation among these sources is often hard to assess. We study robustly optimal strategies—those that maximize the worst-case payoff guarantee across all correlation structures. With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy is strikingly simple: use only the best information source and ignore the rest. With more actions, a robustly optimal strategy decomposes the problem into local comparisons and assigns each comparison to the source that is best at that comparison. With more states, the same specialization logic survives through a concavification characterization: the decision problem is decomposed into payoff-relevant components, and each component is assigned to its best source. These results offer a new rationale for why ignoring information can be optimal and highlight the benefit of using specialized information sources when correlations are ambiguous.
focus_rationale: This is a theoretical decision-theory paper on robust aggregation of information sources under ambiguous correlation, with no specific economy studied.

title: When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE?
abstract: In this paper I revisit the interpretation of the linear instrumental variables (IV) estimand as a weighted average of conditional local average treatment effects (LATEs). I focus on a situation in which additional covariates are required for identification while the reduced-form and first-stage regressions may be misspecified due to an implicit homogeneity restriction on the effects of the instrument. I show that the weights on some conditional LATEs are negative and the IV estimand is no longer interpretable as a causal effect under a weaker version of monotonicity, i.e. when there are compliers but no defiers at some covariate values and defiers but no compliers elsewhere. The problem of negative weights disappears in the interacted specification of Angrist and Imbens (I1995), which avoids misspecification and seems to be underused in applied work. I illustrate my findings in an application to the causal effects of pretrial detention on case outcomes. In this setting, I reject the stronger version of monotonicity, demonstrate that the interacted instruments are sufficiently strong for consistent estimation using the jackknife methodology, and present several estimates that are economically and statistically different, depending on whether the interacted instruments are used.
focus_rationale: A methodological paper on interpreting linear IV estimands with an empirical illustration on pretrial detention in US criminal cases; it has no particular focus on either advanced or emerging economies.

title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
abstract: Economists and historians have long debated how open-access areas, frontier regions, and customary landholding regimes transformed into private property. This paper analyzes decentralized enclosure processes using the theory of aggregative games, examining how population density, enclosure costs, potential productivity gains, and local governance capacity, including the power to demand compensation, jointly determine the mix of property regimes. Depending on these fundamentals, private decisions to enclose may be strategic complements or substitutes. Strategic complements generate tipping points and socially destructive property races, whereas strategic substitutes produce smoother transitions and may leave enclosure below the social optimum. While policies to strengthen customary governance or compensate displaced stakeholders can realign incentives, addressing one distortion while neglecting others can worsen welfare.
focus_rationale: This is a theoretical model of land enclosure using aggregative games, with no particular economy studied; it is historical and general in application.

title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
abstract: Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums.
